I took a look at the clauses. I will point out the main risks regarding making these clauses mutual:

# If 9.3 were to be made mutual, then this would mean that Bolt may have to pay a contractual penalty of 10,000 EUR to DTLi if Bolt were to breach the confidentiality obligation (clause 9.1) or the obligation related to the designation of the goods (clause 9.2).
# Section 10 is a bit more tricky because the second and third subsections relate to claims that result in the acts or omissions of the Supplier, but the first subsection does not have that limitation. If the second and third subsections were to made mutual, then Bolt may have to compensate DTLi for essentially all damages that +Bolt is liable for+ and that result from third party claims against DTLi relating to the supply of the goods. However, if the first subsection were to also be made mutual, then this would mean that whenever a third party files an intellectual property claim against DTLi, then Bolt would have to indemnify DTLi, but if the third party files the claim against Bolt, then DTLi would have to indemnify Bolt - therefore making the first subsection mutual would not make sense in practice.

Making these clauses mutual would mean that Bolt will assume the above risks. Ideally Bolt would not assume such risks. While this is legally OK, it is more a business decision.

If DTLi insists on making the clauses mutual, I would offer the following alternative:

# Remove clause 9.3 (this way Bolt would not be able to demand a contractual penalty, but neither would DTLi), and
# Make clause 10 mutual, but re-word the first subsection as follows:

{quote}any claim made against {color:#ff5630}one party{color} for actual or alleged infringement of a third party's intellectual property rights arising out of, or in connection with, the supply or use of the goods,{color:#ff5630} to the extent that the infringement is attributable to the acts or omissions of the other party, its employees, agents or subcontractors{color};{quote}

Please note that if section 10 were to made mutual, then the rest of the section must also be re-worded (I currently only provided wording for the first subsection).

Let me know how you wish to proceed and if you have any comments regarding the above.

Hey [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] / [~accountid:602f9aeb871d30006843505c] 👋  - I’ve been working a lot on much the wider piece re: global holistic assessments (🌎). I’ve now set out my thoughts on this below.

[~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897]  - have a look through / take this on board to provide your local specific advice to [~accountid:602f9aeb871d30006843505c] 👍 

+*_Quick summary_*+

* *_There_* +*_is_*+ *_scope to decide this on a per market basis._*
* *_Acceptance rate metrics are not recommended._*
* *_Using Driver Score 1.0 / completion rate / passenger ratings requirements_* +*_is_*+ *_possible if Bolt can accept some risk._*
* *_Using a combination of_* +*_completion rate / passenger ratings_*+ *_is the least riskiest type of implementation._*

----

{color:#4c9aff}+*_Overview - category access requirements:_*+{color}

* How markets set-up categories can be decided on a per-market basis. Whenever there are requirements based on ‘performance scoring’, Bolt should always consider how it's intending to rationalise this.
* The best narratives are generally always along the lines of _"matching the right rider with the right driver"_ <-- Bolt has to draw a line somewhere to ensure that there can be a correct match :green-check: 
* Which asks the question: *_how can Bolt externally justify access criteria or any other criteria?_*
* For example of how we can logically justify using cancellations rates, see this webpage on [{color:#ff5630}+*scheduled rides*+{color}|https://bolt.eu/en/support/articles/81554/].
* Keep in mind that in applying criteria to categories, you’re effectively applying them to all drivers that have the ability to enter to category (even if they don’t meet those thresholds).
* If Bolt wants to distance itself from reclassification scrutiny, it ideally doesn’t want to be seen to locking ‘higher earning work' behind ‘Bolt’s own performance targets’ / ‘Bolt’s ongoing automated data assessments’. This can be weaponised as ‘locking bonuses behind ongoing Leapsome-like reviews’.
* Bolt generally ought to its own assessment on whether guardrails actually impact GMV performance, rather than looking to ‘simply follow its competitors’ (even though looking at our competitors can be helpful). Do these guardrails actually inform performance? Is there any way that the same outcome can be achieved without increasing risk? Does Bolt +_need_+ to stack performance guardrails already used in the market onto new feature / initiatives? etc.

----

{color:#4c9aff}+*_The impact of using ‘performance criteria’ for feature access:_*+{color}

Our ‘global assessment’ of how category access requirements may impact Bolt’s ability to defend against reclassification claims / regulator action (+*_if_*+ that happens) is set out below. This assumes claims are made by capable lawyers.

!Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.00.png|width=89.10056591883912%,alt="Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.00.png"!

!Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.08.png|width=89.10056591883912%,alt="Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.08.png"!

{color:#97a0af}_Note: this extract is from the tool that will be used to assess EU markets in H2 in anticipation of the rollout of the PWD._{color}

Using AR thresholds (or online hour requirements) for category access, incentive targets or similar is considered the ‘highest risk’ as it can be used to argue that there is an ‘obligation to work'. It’s very difficult to rationalise.

Of course, sensitivities +*are*+ always market specific and the overall risk assessment for a market should be holistic (taking all factor and operational practices into account).

----

{color:#4c9aff}+*_(For reference only) the impact of using ‘acceptance rate blocking / driver score 1.0 blocking):_*+{color}

!Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.00.png|width=89.1%,alt="Screenshot 2024-08-13 at 12.30.00.png"!

[~accountid:612f31d89976c300693ebaf7]{color:#4c9aff} +*_comments re: ES proposal:_*+{color}{color:#4c9aff}  {color}🇪🇸 

* Unless there is an ES specific narrative that can be identified and well-reasoned regarding acceptance rates, this is not recommended.
* I don’t think that those Uber messages expressly refer to acceptance rate…? Then again, I don’t speak Spanish very well 🙂 
* Using +driver score 1.0+, +completion rate+ and +passenger ratings+ _could_ be justified along the following lines if the local market can accept some risk:
** _"Riders who request premium category expect a more comfortably journey. These riders have higher expectation of a quality vehicle and a premium service. For that reason, the premium category is therefore only available to drivers that: (i) have a premium vehicle (ii) do not have a recent history of feedback that indicates a non-premium standard of service (driver score: [X]  / completion rate [X]_ _/ passenger ratings [X])."_
* Using completion rates is more justifiable than to using Driver Score 1.0 as the latter combines various signals and as more akin to an ‘ongoing Leapsome-like’ assessment. However, there is scope to take a view and use Driver Score 1.0 if that is already being used in the market.
* Just FYI - Driver Score 1.0 is currently being reworked into a less sensitive version (codename: Driver Score 2.0) As DS2.0 will no longer give drivers a ‘score’ in app, it could not be used to ‘gatekeep’ feature access in the same way. As and when this happens, the relevant metrics for feature access will need to move to other metrics e.g. completion rate. 
* It’ll be worth double-checking with the privacy team that using these metrics in this context is acceptable under the current privacy notice.
* The follow will apply under PWD: {color:#ff5630}_“Any decision to restrict, suspend or terminate the contractual relationship or the account of_{color}
{color:#ff5630}_a person performing platform work or any other decision of equivalent detriment shall be taken by a human being.”_{color} - this appears to apply to removing drivers from categories. How Bolt will practically deal with this under PWD is under review (⚙️).

Hi[~accountid:62bbfa39ec4c0d377f9fc3b7] 

I completed a legal assessment for launching Bolt Send and have not identified any specific blocks.

Bolt Send would fall under the regulation of the [Tiekuljetussopimuslaki|https://www.finlex.fi/fi/laki/ajantasa/1979/19790345] (Road Transport Contract Act) which, inter alia, applies to contracts for the transport of goods by motor vehicle in Finland (_domestic transport_ within the meaning of the Act). Among other things, the Act regulates, to an extent, the rights and obligations of the contracting parties (Chapter 3), liability of the carrier (Chapter 4) etc. However, the Act does say that in domestic transport the provisions of this law cannot be deviated from, unless the exceptional quality of the goods or transport or other special circumstances make it reasonable (Section 5 of Chapter 1). As such, we may have to make some changes to the T&Cs if there are any non-conformities with the law, but may have the option of deviating from the law, if it is reasonable.

One thing worth noting is that based on the Act, Finnish regulations seem to follow the logic that the transport of goods is generally accompanied by a *waybill* (even in domestic transport). The waybill is essentially regarded as the transport contract, it acts as the main proof of the agreed upon conditions (description of goods, destination etc) and both the sender and recipient are entitled to demand that the carrier provides them with the waybill. The waybill can be electronic, but must contain, among other things, the number of parcels +and their special marks and numbers or a corresponding description of the goods+ and +the total weight of the goods or its quantity expressed in another way+ (Section 8 of Chapter 2).

However, in case of domestic transport, the waybill is not required if the parties agree so, or if drawing up a waybill causes special inconvenience, or it is not a practice for the transport in question (Section 6 of Chapter 2). Since, to my understanding, collecting the above info (description of goods, total weight) is not part of Bolt Send, we won’t be able to draft a waybill which meets minimum requirements of the law.

Considering the above, I propose two alternatives:

# Not draft a waybill and expressly state this in our T&Cs. This way we would rely on the exception that the parties can agree on not using a waybill for domestic transport (Section 6 of Chapter 2). Additionally, we can argue that drawing up a waybill causes special inconvenience AND it is not a practice for the transport in question (the last part would however need to be confirmed with some further research); or
# Arrange that general info regarding the transport be sent to the client’s e-mail (thus drafting an electronic waybill), but not trouble ourselves with specific information such as the description of goods or the total weight by relying on the exception that domestic transport may deviate from the law, if it is reasonable (Section 5 of Chapter 1).

Personally, I suggest going with the first alternative and expressly stating in our T&Cs that, considering the functionalities of the Bolt platform, both the client and the driver agree not the draw up a waybill. However, do you see a reclass risk here? Bolt would essentially regulate an important part of the transport contract which Bolt is not a party to. 

Let me know your thoughts.

*Declaration of continued employment*
You must complete this section in the case of a fixed-term or temporary employment contract.
o The section must be completed in full;
o the section must be signed separately and also have a company stamp. If you do not
have a company stamp, you should declare it on company letterhead. This declaration
must be signed by the same person who also signs the employer's statement.
*Income*
o Gross annual salary must equal 12 times the salary listed on the submitted
payslip, or 13 times if there is a four-weekly salary.
A common situation is that the employer's statement already takes into account a
future salary increase. If this is the case, please state on company letterhead
as of when the increase takes effect and that the increase is irrevocable.
Another point to note is that the actual salary should be entered, so in the case of part-timers, not the salary based on full time.
o The vacation allowance is calculated as stated in the employment contract, so for example as 8% of the Gross annual salary. For vacation vouchers, the total value of the vouchers should be entered over the past 12 months.
o If there is structural irregularity pay, commission and/or overtime, then enter in the
total benefit for the past 12 months.
There are banks that allow a greater number of months to be counted. Your employee
or the mortgage broker will then have to indicate that to you.
"Structural," by the way, means that it is common knowledge that irregularity, commission or overtime is is part of the job.
o A fixed benefit, such as a 13th month or year-end bonus, is fixed if it is unconditionally agreed upon in the employment contract.
o If item 8. is entered, please also include 4) after the description (see footnote 4).
*Loans/wage attachment*
o A private loan or wage garnishment will usually not be involved. Nevertheless, we request you also to please complete this section completely.
*Signature*
o The signature must be complete and include a company stamp. If you do not have a
company stamp, you should declare it on company letterhead. This statement must be signed by the same person who also signs the employer's statement.

Hi [~accountid:63cfbe91c565900ff404f491] - I see you have messaged asking each of the following (apologies, but for some reason I am only notified of this by email, and it has not appeared on this ticket on my end):

* “_Could we ask drivers to fill out a form with their email if they would like to be invited to the event? We will randomly select drivers from the list and omit the competitions. It would be enough for us, we just want to make this event and invite drivers, we can skip competitions, ratings._”
* “_can we just leave a competition for the most rides and we will not collect any data, just will check which drivers made the most rides? What should we do to start the invitation?_”

I include my thoughts on both of these options below.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
{color:#403294}*IN SUMMARY:*{color}

* {color:#4c9aff}*Can you confirm whether the sweepstake will be governed by any sort of agreement*{color}? This impacts our advice as it affects what legal justification we can rely on to process the drivers' data in this context. If given the option, it would be preferable to be able to rely on some form of agreement here.
* {color:#36b37e}*Of the two options, the first is preferable*{color} from a privacy perspective, as it would be a more transparent approach and would ensure that Bolt has a clearer legal justification for processing the data (given that the drivers are effectively opting-in to the sweepstake).
* {color:#ff5630}*We do not recommend taking the second option*{color}, as it raises a few issues in terms of legal justification and transparency.
{panel}

----

+*Option A - Random selection (i.e., ask drivers to fill out the form, and then randomly selection from the list)*+

* {color:#36b37e}*Of the two options, this seems to be the most viable*{color}. This is because the drivers will be informed about the processing before it happens in the email and form (and they are effectively opting-in to the sweepstake), which helps us to get around certain issues relating to legal justification and transparency (see Option B below for further details).
* We should still ensure that we are _emailing_ the drivers with the form, rather than _calling_ them.
* Even if we are randomly selecting drivers, {color:#4c9aff}*can you confirm whether the sweepstake will be governed by some sort of agreement*{color} (e.g. the [+Campaign T&C+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ybRlet8ae-IPsv5T7MemwjSEYiNGi0afYS5DQS3Nzb8/edit] apply to randomly picking a winner from those who apply, even though they involve providing the winner with a prize rather than inviting them to an event)?
** *If it* +*will*+ *be governed by an agreement*: We need to make sure that collecting the driver’s name and email for the purpose of determining who will be invited to the event is mentioned in the agreement (the agreement should also be clear that ‘winners' will be picked via random allocation). We would also need to ensure that the transparency wording drafted below is included in the form.
** *If it* +*will not*+ *be governed by an agreement:* We will need to consider and change our advice on legal basis / transparency wording. This may raise some issues, and so if possible {color:#4c9aff}*it would be preferable for us to be able to rely on some form of agreement here*{color}, but please let us know either way.

----

+*Option B - Rides competition (i.e., do not ask drivers to fill out the form, but check the driver that completed the most rides)*+

* {color:#ff5630}*We do not recommend taking this approach*{color}, as this presents a few difficulties in terms of the legal justification that Bolt can rely on in this context as well as transparency / fairness.
* *Legal basis*: Bolt must rely on a specific legal justification set out in data protection law to process drivers' completed rides information for this purpose. Of the main legal bases that _could_ apply here, the following are difficult to justify:
** *Consent*: It would be difficult to argue that Bolt relies on the driver’s consent to process their number of completed rides for this purpose, as at no point has the driver specifically consented to this. We advise against this approach.
** *Contractual necessity*: If this competition is governed by an agreement (as above, {color:#4c9aff}*please confirm*{color}), Bolt could try and argue that processing the driver’s number of completed rides is necessary for selecting a winner per the terms of that agreement. However, the issue here is that it would be difficult to argue that the driver ever signed up to the agreement in any way. As such, we advise against this approach.
** *Legitimate interest*: We could try and argue that Bolt has a legitimate interest in conducting sweepstakes to deepen our existing relationship with our drivers / develop new ones, and that processing the driver’s number of completed rides is necessary for pursuing this interest. However, the issue here is that the drivers must be allowed the opportunity to object to the processing of their personal data for this purpose - since this competition will only be lasting for the next few weeks, it is foreseeable that some drivers may subsequently complain that they were never given an opportunity to opt-out. Also, we would need to conduct a legitimate interest assessment, which is further uplift.
* *Transparency*: In any case, Bolt would need to make sure that drivers are informed that their number of completed rides will be processed in the context of this competition +*before*+ such processing takes place. This is because such processing is not currently mentioned in the live Driver Privacy Notice. We could theoretically send an email to all drivers with some transparency wording that notifies them about the processing, but this raises the following issues:
** The net result of this approach would not massively differ from Option A (as we will still need to send an initial email to the drivers) - given the issues already flagged, Option A therefore still seems preferable.
** As mentioned above, drivers should be given the opportunity to opt-out of this competition. Sending the transparency wording may lead to a wave of opt-out requests in a very short window.
** We would need to include in the email clear wording on how the winner would be determined. Otherwise, any drivers that did not ‘win’ may question exactly how the ‘winners’ were determined (the likelihood of this happening is low, but possible).

Providing dash cams to drivers in Paraguay could potentially increase the risk of reclassification, as it might be seen as providing work equipment, which is typically the responsibility of an employer. However, given the currently low reclassification risk in Paraguay and the pressure/blackmail from authorities to implement these cameras for driver safety, proceeding with the proposed pilot project involving 50 drivers seems reasonable.

That said, I would advise against expanding the project beyond the pilot phase. Instead, it would be more prudent to incorporate the dash cams into the Bolt Offer program. This would allow drivers who wish to install these cameras to do so through third-party providers potentially at more competitive prices.

For the pilot phase, please ensure that we do not have access to the recordings and that riders are clearly informed they are being recorded. Additionally, if installing the cameras requires sharing drivers' personal data, such as license plates, with the company providing the dash cams, please ensure that a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) is in place and coordinate with the privacy team accordingly.

Hey! Just to add some context here, the cashback we are talking about longer term is not real money, but credits. 

Background of it is here in this doc, the features final details are still in scoping, but on a high level I copied the split of Balance below. 

tl;dr; — these credits (and also the cashback given) is not a payment method as Balance is, but a discount on a future purchase instead. Balance as a payment method will remain a separate thing. 

[https://docs.google.com/document/d/1D1i4alRG7sA1kztEmaIsn8mnY_xXQN_O9R5cqleEDRk/edit#heading=h.yrfwwprk9ip1|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1D1i4alRG7sA1kztEmaIsn8mnY_xXQN_O9R5cqleEDRk/edit#heading=h.yrfwwprk9ip1|smart-link] 

*Copied from the doc:* 

* *Where we have to navigate in:*
** Balance today = legally non-regulated “incentives” which we (ab)use to do actual refunds, top-ups etc 
** What is okay 
*** Giving refunds, cashbacks, etc to the balance — legally we can defend that these are just incentives to be used not actual real money
** What is not okay
*** Top-ups, actual money mixed with incentives 
*** Only in certain markets where we are licenses to handle funds, like Netherlands and Belgium, do we allow for topup 
**** Problem there is that we officially have a payment account, but could use it for incentives too which might not be actual money
** Other things going on:
*** We’re cleaning up the house a lot and can't have messy accounting and finances if we are preparing for an IPO at some point :) 
*** This is why we have big initiatives like the ledger, revamping all the flows how money moves etc going on 



* *So, what this means for Balance and expiring cashbacks* 
** Makes sense to split this into a
*** Payment account — actual real money that is regulated
*** Credits — do-what-you-want incentives which are not regulated 
*** To the user we can still show “you have 9.84€ available”, but if they for example open up the Balance page, they see a breakdown where
**** 5€ is actual money 
**** 3€ is credit expiring in 2 weeks
**** 1.84€ is credit expiring  in 2 days (which was 3€ when issued)
**** 4€ credits have already expired 2 days ago 
**** _Note — UX for this for competitors like Uber is crap, I think we can make this nice and understandable :)_ 
** Why
*** You can’t expire real money, it is questionable to block it between different use cases etc. 
*** Easier to roll out, credits we can do wherever however, payment account left only for those markets where we can do it 
*** If we do something that is in between right now, we would have to rebuild it in Q3/Q4 again anyways 
*** Using separate Credits would allow us to do all the things we have wanted:
**** Limit to specific verticals, specific stores even, have them expire, whatever we want. 
**** Or give expiring credits instead of refunds for example (unless customer is explicit in getting real money back

Hi [~accountid:712020:f989ec0f-bf00-4c9b-be89-cc44499bb288] ,

Thanks for raising the ticket. Please find below the requirements to validly suspend / terminate drivers account, according to the Platform Work Directive (EU) and to the Social Dialogue agreement on blockings conditions. 

Please note that the Social Dialogue agreement on blockings frames suspensions due to low rating and requires the platform to provide transparent information upfront, send warnings via email and send an email notification upon the suspension. 



# *Transparent information:* this point is respected as drivers can access the information on this online page: [+https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/support/articles/72174/+|https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/support/articles/72174/] 
# *Human review before blocking*: in the EU, the platform must ensure that an individual reviews each case before a Driver’s account is permanently terminated. However, a temporary suspension does not require prior human review. 
# *Email messaging before and upon blocking*: the platform must deliver durable medium notifications to Drivers upon suspension, termination and upon each breach of T&Cs that could entail suspension/termination if repeated (warnings). 

* For warnings, please use the templates set [+here+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1dwsUcDxvPq4LNZ1BN32mLyMWFBy3DQZBZdYZS3nkUtE/edit]. 

* For emails informing of the block, please make sure that the email sets out:

# the first date the block is effective
# the duration of the suspension
# the applicable ‘Approved Blocking Reason’
# how the service provider can make a business user complaint 

Please note that in France, there must be a 48 hours delay between the email warning of the suspension and the email informing of the suspension.

*4. Before being suspended, the driver must have an opportunity to comment on the decision*: this must be respected in France according to the Dialogue social, and the formalities regarding how the driver can send their comment must be set in the email informing them (please refer to paragraph 3 above).

Hi [~accountid:63622ea17d4645af4f03bd18] - I would be grateful for your thoughts on this one.

*Context:*

* A law firm (Mooneerams - Personal Injury Solicitors) has written to us on behalf of a rider ([Ilaria Giudiceandrea|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/users/user/169684537]), asking for the full name and address of a driver (who we have identified as [Dean Radford|https://admin.bolt.eu/fleet/Drivers/driver/3836250]).
* The law firm wants this information strictly for the purpose of issuing legal proceedings against the driver. The full wording of the law firm’s request is [here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/416554351].
* Having done some digging, it seems that the legal proceedings are the result of an incident during an [order|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/467859293/129?orderTryId=718138126] on 14 September 2023. The rider was injured during the trip (the driver shut the boot on her head) and the driver had to drop her off at A&E. The rider incurred hundreds of pounds as a result.
* The rider has raised concerns with Bolt about this in the past (see e.g., [here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/271495861]) and threatened to get personal injury lawyers involved (which is what is happening here - albeit against the driver).
* The law firm are making the request for the driver’s information under Schedule 2, Para 5 of the DPA 2018 (Information required to be disclosed by law etc or in connection with legal proceedings) - in particular, it seems, Para 5(3).

*My Thoughts:*

* I have done some quick research on this (as I have not seen this provision used in this way before), and it appears that Bolt _can_ disclose the driver’s information per the exception under Schedule 2, Para 5(3), but it is not _mandatory_ and should always be assessed on a case-by-case basis / decided on the merits. In any event, we should also ensure that any information we are sharing is strictly _necessary_, and that Bolt has a legal basis for sharing the information.
* On balance, *I think we should share the requested information*, because:
** The data being requested is limited (i.e., surname and address - we could even just provide name and _email address_ if you think that would be more appropriate), and arguably necessary for the purpose for which it is requested (issuing legal proceedings).
** I have googled the law firm / [requestor|https://www.mooneerams.com/meet-the-team/ffion-palmer/] and they seem legitimate.
** The rider has previously raised concerns with Bolt and been frustrated by our responses. In spite of this, the rider is only taking action against the driver, so we should try to not frustrate the rider further.
** The reason for the request seems fair - the rider’s injuries look serious, and they only had access to the driver’s first name. We should not be seen to be thwarting the rider’s right to pursue the driver in court if they want to.
** I think the most appropriate legal basis here seems to be legitimate interest (i.e., Bolt’s legitimate interest in upholding the right to legal redress).
* We should also ensure that the response does not refer to the driver as “our employee”, as this is incorrect.

*Questions:*

* Have you seen requests like this before, and if so is there a particular process by which they are handled?
* Should I loop in anyone else from the wider legal team?
* Do you agree with the approach of sharing the requested information? If so, I will prepare some draft wording.

Hey [~accountid:5b4700d3fd94c32c014fa95f]!

FYI, we were able to correct Issue 1 without opening the previous period. Below are the steps we took:

# We unreconciled the bank statement line from 01/11/2023.
# Then, we canceled the intercompany receipts from 01/11/2023. This created operational journals in the first open period, which is currently 01/08/2024.
# We recorded a new intercompany receipt: first for the smaller amount (430,609.00 RON) and then for the larger amount (4,163,691.00 RON). This created new operational journals as of 01/08/2024. Therefore, there was no impact on the balance sheet, as the total amount of the movements is zero.
# We confirmed that:

* The Trial Balance now matches the Receivables Aging Details.
* Invoice C-RO001-23-000051 appears as fully paid.
* The Receivables Aging contains only unpaid invoices from 2024.

All in all, it seems that the error occurred because, while creating the intercompany receipt for the larger amount, all items were selected, including (142,609.00) RON and (288,000.00) RON, which should have remained only as part of the smaller amount. Unfortunately, I did not realize to take a screenshot of this, but while creating the intercompany receipt, it automatically selected all available items, even if some had already been used for another intercompany receipt.

As I can see from the process history, we did not cancel the receipt for the larger amount back in November. Therefore, re-recording the intercompany receipt for the smaller amount at that time had no effect. I think it’s important to keep in mind that if there are multiple intercompany receipts, the smaller amounts should be recorded first to avoid such situations in the future.

I hope this knowledge sharing is helpful to your team as well. 😊 🌻

Hi Mariana,

Workday splits absence into two: *time off* and *leave of absence*.

The report mentioned only returns time off, this is used normally for annual leave and other leaves that you take by day. There are a few paternity types configured as time off.

Leave of absence on the other hand is used for long term leaves, like maternity, and it has an estimated last day of leave, not booked by days. When placed on this leave, workers have (On leave) next to name in Workday.

Time off and leave of absence results cannot be grouped into same report due to their differences in requesting it.

For that please use “Workers on leave” report.

Hi, [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] 

I am happy to announce that we finally received a response from Circle K regarding the Data Sharing Agreement. 
Please find their answer as follows: 


_I've attached to this e-mail Bolt's DPA with a few new comments from my side._

 

_Regarding the joint/independent controllership, I understand Bolt's perspective, and it makes sense for the majority of the commercial relationship. However, based on the factual relationship between Bolt and CK, it appears that they act as joint controllers specifically when it comes to the relationship between the use of cards and discounts for drivers:_

 

# _Joint determination of purposes and means:_
## _Both Bolt and CK are involved in deciding the purpose and means of processing personal data for the loyalty program. CK provides the benefits, while Bolt handles the communication and distribution of loyalty cards to drivers. This collaborative effort indicates that both parties have a say in how and why the data is processed._
# _Shared responsibilities:_

# _The responsibilities laid out in the Agreement show that Bolt and CK need to work together to make the program successful. For example, CK sets the discount limitations, but any changes to these limitations must be communicated and coordinated with Bolt. This demonstrates shared decision-making and management of the program._

# _Interdependence:_

# _The success of the loyalty program in the context of Bolt-CK relationship relies on both parties working together. CK depends on Bolt to reach out to drivers and distribute the loyalty cards, while Bolt depends on CK's program to offer attractive benefits to its drivers. This interdependence shows that neither party can run the program effectively without the other, indicating joint control over the data processing activities._

# _Coordination on changes:_

# _Any changes to the loyalty program, such as adjustments to discount limitations, require coordination between Bolt and CK. This ongoing need for coordination shows that both parties are involved in managing and implementing the program within the limits of their commercial relationship, further supporting the idea of joint controllership._

 

_In summary, the factual relationship between Bolt and CK involves converging decision-making, shared responsibilities, interdependence, and coordinated actions. These factors collectively indicate that Bolt and CK act as joint controllers under the GDPR. This perspective seems to be supported by recent CJEU decisions such as C-40/17, C‑683/21, and C‑231/22._

 

_Of course, both companies are independent controllers in all activities preceding and following the distribution of the loyalty cards: Bolt is independently responsible for collecting the drivers' data, just as it is independently responsible for what happens after such collection when acting for its own purposes. Similarly, CK is independently responsible if, for example, it uses the card's consumption data to achieve its own commercial objectives. As stated in case C-40/17, point 74, "a natural or legal person may be a controller [...] jointly with others only in respect of operations involving the processing of personal data for which it determines jointly the purposes and means. By contrast [...] that natural or legal person cannot be considered to be a controller [...] in the context of operations that precede or are subsequent in the overall chain of processing for which that person does not determine either the purposes or the means."_

 

_This is why I recommend both companies be considered as joint controllers in this situation. But as usual, the final decision should come from the business._

*_Matheus Passos Silva_*

_Data Protection Officer Europe_

_Circle K_

* Here is the [original agreement |https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WqqmIJ_qYClgo14FzHbKbZPUqj0vz0zM/view?usp=sharing]which covers the period from 26 January 2022 to 26 April 2022
* There have been multiple renewals which can be found [here|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/15jIh5BktMO-1WIAuM103Fih9NmGljHE1?usp=sharing] (still missing the addendums for period between October 1, 2023 and 26 January 2024)
* The [ |https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JeejsFzwnEiaOeIWkgFtRmx5OqJBKz4P/view?usp=sharing][+last renewal was signed+|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JeejsFzwnEiaOeIWkgFtRmx5OqJBKz4P/view?usp=sharing] on January 24, 2024 and covering the period between February 1, 2024 to January 31, 2025
* In the case of the expansion markets, we signed addendums which referred to the original for [ |https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LaHMjPT1czMd3vLcgQz6iT2jCI1gnfEO/view?usp=sharing][+Malaysia+|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LaHMjPT1czMd3vLcgQz6iT2jCI1gnfEO/view?usp=sharing] &[ |https://drive.google.com/file/d/1L1rrcwvqq4Zh_uLpsBP21ls9N6C2RkHK/view?usp=sharing][+Vietnam+|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1L1rrcwvqq4Zh_uLpsBP21ls9N6C2RkHK/view?usp=sharing]
* Finance did raise concerns as to why Bolt Ops OU was paying the bills for TH and not the local entity and also what the plan is for expansion markets about who should pay
* The decision agreed on was that the current TH contract that expires on 31 January, 2025 will continue to serve as the master contract. Bolt OPs OU will continue to pay AGA for all the different work streams linked to the addendums. 
* Towards expiration of the contract we will then negotiate and sign a new global master contract between AGA and Bolt Ops OU. The contract will include sub-contracts with each legal entity and split the fee country by country and have each local entity pays AGA. In  the case of expansion markets, the addendum will specify that Bolt Ops OU will pay AGA for these until after creation of local entity and launch.

Hi [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] - as discussed on today’s call, I think there is a level of ambiguity to the user’s follow-up to us providing them with their data (i.e., “_The data provided does not include clarity on the rider ratings. I have reason to believe that some ratings were not in good faith and indeed are related to driver caused incidents_”). In my view, “_clarity on the rider ratings_” could be interpreted as a request for either:

* Each specific rider rating that the rider has ever received; or
* An explanation on the process / mechanics of rider ratings.

Admittedly, the rider is more likely to be after the first option, however I would still argue that this is unclear. In order to make sure that we are not oversharing information unnecessarily, I would suggest the following approach {color:#4c9aff}*- do you agree?* {color}

[~accountid:63622ea17d4645af4f03bd18] - I would also be grateful for your eyes on this (background is below in the status update). My view here is that we should only consider providing rider ratings if +explicitly+ requested to do so (which arguably has not yet happened here) - {color:#36b37e}*what do you think of the approach below*{color}? If you agree with the approach, we can leverage the language in Step 1 for any future requests of a similar nature 🙂 

----

*Step 1:*

Respond to the rider with the following in good time. Crucially, we are quoting the rider directly so that we have just cause for interpreting the request in the way that we have. Also, so as to not seem obstructive, we are inviting the rider to clarify that specific rider ratings is what they are after - that way, if they confirm this, we can at least be confident that we are providing information that has been specifically requested.

_Dear Thomas,_

_Thank you for your request for “clarity on the rider ratings_”. _Please note that rider ratings as they appear in your Bolt app are calculated as an average rating based on your ratings from the previous 365 days. Each rating is from 1 to 5, as provided by the driver at the end of each trip. Further information on rider ratings can be found here:_ [_https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/_|https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/] _._

_If you require specific information concerning rider ratings, we would be grateful if you could please clarify it so that our specialist team can consider the request accordingly._

_Yours sincerely,_

*_Bolt_*

----

*Step 2:*

I think it is likely that the rider will respond demanding each specific rider rating. Once they have done so, we could provide them with a table that looks similar to [this|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1_XHCTADNZkgr3ox9A8L97mk-EN4ZoOpDdctnpgROvZ0/edit?gid=237079376#gid=237079376] (i.e., the table just lists the date / time of each order, and the rider rating given. It does not include the driver’s name, nor any locations). This way, we are minimising the risk posed to the drivers themselves that provided these ratings.

In our response to be sent with this table, we can make it explicitly clear that we need to take the rights of the drivers into account, hence why we have removed so much information. If the user does not like this, then I think we have a reasonably strong position to push back and say that we have discharged our obligations under privacy laws, and so there is nothing further that we can do.

Dear António,

Thank you for submitting your data subject rights request to Bolt. We understand from the wording of your request (“_I do not authorise the disclosure of my personal data”_) that you are objecting to +*all*+ sharing of your personal data by Bolt.

We are committed to responding to your request in a timely and efficient manner. However, in order to process your request, we require additional information. In particular, please specify *which of Bolt’s specific data processing activities / data processing purposes you are objecting to*.

+*Why is this important?*+

The right to object under Article 21 of the General Data Protection Regulation is not absolute, and does not apply to all data processing activities that Bolt conducts.

In particular, you may have the right to object if Bolt is processing your personal data on the basis of Bolt’s *legitimate interests*, but not where Bolt relies on other legal bases (for example, consent or the performance of a contract). As set out in our Privacy Notice ([https://bolt.eu/pt-pt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/pt-pt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]), Bolt relies on different legal bases for processing your personal data depending on the processing activity. As such, your objection request cannot be applied to every data processing activity that Bolt conducts (including all sharing of your personal data by Bolt).

+*Next Steps*+

Please be aware that we are unable to respond to your request until we receive the additional information specified above. The deadline of one month to respond to your request will be paused until we have received the additional information.

We appreciate your cooperation in this matter and look forward to receiving the requested information from you.

Yours sincerely 

*Bolt*

# considering the above, we would not be exchanging any data with them yet, apart from details needed to prepare and conclude the contract.
# the T&C are vague and too general in part of data protection - Section 13 (attached here[^Terms of Business LLP Sep 2022 (1).pdf] ). BDO may act both as a data controller or a processor - but the scope of data processing is not clarified.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*For data controller part (C2C)*, the obligations for Bolt and BDO are generally very limited. The clause would generally require Bolt to ensure lawfulness of the transfer, transparency for data subjects whose data is transferred, and an obligation to reasonably cooperate.
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*For data processor part (C2P)*, it does not tick some of the requirements under Art. 28 of the GDPR. Example: no list of subprocessors provided, no clear procedure for engagement and change of sub-processors, no clear TOMs indicated. Also - it does not comply with our standards (Bolt bears costs for all assistance by BDO, including DSRs, complying with obligations under the GDPR like DPIAs, etc.
{panel}

*Confirmed approach:*

* *the T&C C2P transfer - our DPA would have to be added and T&C clarified in this regard* (considering BDO will likely be processor and the services will include personal data). It's easier to provide a DPA and spend less time updating the T&C, as the contract is low value, and no data transfer is happening right now - only potentially when the services are provided.
* *For C2C transfer - clarify the scope of their processing activities first, and then decide if a DSA is strictly necessary*. For C2C, it should not be essential by law, and basic clauses are already included.

*Deadline:* no strict deadline for the privacy input and not top priority for business, but best to add the input promptly. Privacy was involved to provide our input 1 week ago.

2] Re/ direct marketing - copying here for visibility:

*1. First party B2C: is soft opt-in possible per the ePrivacy Directive Article 13(2), or does hard opt-in apply?*

Under Art. 11(1) of Law 3471/2006 (Art. 13 par. 1 of e-Privacy Directive), unsolicited communications for the purposes of direct marketing of goods or services, or any advertising purposes are not permitted by any means of electronic communications without human intervention (including e-mail) unless the controller/sender has previously obtained the explicit consent of the recipient (hard opt-in)
As regards unsolicited communications with human intervention (calls), they are not permitted, if the subscriber has stated to the provider of the publicly available electronic communications service that he/she does not wish to accept such communications in general. The provider must enter these statements in a special subscriber directory, which shall be at the subscriber's disposal, free of charge (opt-out). 
By way of derogation, Art. 11(3) of Law 3471/2006 (Art. 13 par. 2 of e-Privacy Directive), provides that where the electronic contact details for electronic mail were legitimately obtained in the context of the sale of a product or a service or other transaction, they may be used for the direct marketing of similar products or services or for the fulfillment of similar purposes, provided that the recipient of the message is given clearly and distinctly the opportunity to object, free of charge and in an easy manner, to such use of electronic contact details at the time of collection of their personal data and in each message, in case the recipient had not initially objected to this use (soft opt-in).
The above provisions apply for unsolicited communications towards both, individuals and legal entities.

*2. First party B2B: is it opt in / opt out consent? Are there guidelines on what is considered B2B direct marketing, and what are the basic rules?*

There is no specific definition of “B2B direct marketing” in the relevant guidelines or legislation. The basic rules are outlined in Law 3471/2006, as mentioned above, in article 13, paragraph 3 of Law 2472/1997, as well as in the HDPA’s decisions on the direct marketing of goods or services and any advertising purposes. Additionally, any email or SMS sent for advertising purposes must include the sender’s or advertiser’s identity and a means for the recipient to object to further communications. Furthermore, emails concerning the direct marketing of goods or services must indicate the commercial nature of the content in the subject line.

*3. B2C/B2B of third party offers: please confirm the consent requirements - i.e., hard opt-in/opt-out. Please clairfy any specific guidelines in this domain if applicable.*

In the case of B2B/B2C direct marketing of third-party offers, the same conditions regarding the provision of recipients' consent, as described above, apply. In any case, the requirement for prior notification of data subjects regarding the processing of their data by both the Data Controller and any third parties/authorized partners to whom the data may be transferred for the purposes of sending direct marketing communications is emphasized.

*4. Enforcement risk for direct marketing on basic level - Low/Medium/High.*

Considering the frequency with which the HDPA issues decisions on cases involving unsolicited communications and direct marketing, and the fact that in these instances the HDPA typically initiates an investigation process following a related complaint by the impacted data subjects, the enforcement risk is classified as "high".

The LOI is preliminary document that expresses the parties' intention to reach an agreement and lay down key terms of the future agreement/contract, but it does not legally bind the parties in the same way as a formal contract. Then I understand that the cashback from the Food orders is to be treated as credits on the Bolt Balance account of the Eater. Additionally, the credit serves as a discount for future purchases, within the same country and within the same vertical.

The reason why I was asking for these details, is to understand the classification and  treatment of this “_cashback on Bolt Balance_” from a legal and tax PoV: 

From the above I can infer that there are specific features of a “Coupon” being granted to the Eater. That is: 1) there is no upfront payment as compared to Single Purpose Voucher (SPV), since there is no prepayment, 2) There is a future discount, 3) Thus, VAT should be applied at coupon redemption (rather than at issuance, as compared to SPVs). This would be the most beneficial approach for Bolt.

Arguments against it being a Coupon, but rather a SPV: 1) there is only 1 specific use for it (i.e. to be redeemed only against a specific type of service - Bolt Food order), and 2) they may create a prepayment liability in our books since they may represent a claim on services (I disregard the accounting treatment, simply pointing this out, since if treated in such manner, it may resemble more to a SPV. It should rather be recognized as a marketing expense when Coupon is redeemed, without previously creating a liability).

Main consequence of this being treated either as a Coupon or a SPV, is the VAT timing and the Accounting implications may change, as described.

The way I see it, for me it looks more like a Coupon, and I would dare to say that the risk of reclassification from one to another is low, but worth to check on the legal classification of Coupons and Vouchers on a country by country basis.

Hi [~accountid:5ad471a8bb811e2b3af9482a] getting back to you from product legal to answer your questions. 

*When promoting BM via email and push notifications to our users, it is important to be aware of antitrust rules* that prohibit agreements between market operators that would restrict competition, and the abuse of dominance. So using safeguard measures is necessary. Please see the file on [+Initial set of rules for targeting Bolt platform users+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-ZJb66nxTKVWqY6lUdsvJsYfd8WOR_lsZsz8Z4yws2c/edit] that need to be applied when doing the promotions. 

# *Promoting Bolt Market to: 1) BM users only, 2) active non-BM users in the Food app, 3) Rider app users, 4) active retail users in the Food app. Content will be focused on promoting Bolt Market value propositions. Branding will be from Bolt Market.*

When promoting Bolt Market to *1) BM users and 2) non BM users* in the Food app, then the customer data used for the promotions should be general (i.e email address and the fact they have/have not ordered from BM is OK), but data such as order frequency and basket content should not be used. More in depth guidelines can be found from the file [+Initial set of rules for targeting Bolt platform users+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-ZJb66nxTKVWqY6lUdsvJsYfd8WOR_lsZsz8Z4yws2c/edit]

When promoting BM to *3) rider app users*, then when they have opted out via their communication preferences from receiving offers about "Bolt`s Products", this should be respected. However, if they have not opted out, then cross-promotion is possible.

When promoting BM to *4) active retail users in the Food app* It is OK to do, as long as the  promotion again is neutral and does not indicate in any way that we have gathered detailed or specific information about users purchasing habits and now we are targeting them based on that information. 

Using BM branding is OK

# *Promoting the Retail/Grocery side of the Food app to: 1) non-retail and non-BM users of the Food app, 2) Rider app users, 3) active retail users. Content will be focused on promoting general retail/grocery value propositions, not mentioning any specific providers. Branding would be from Bolt Food.*

Same answer as for Q1. All of it is OK to do, as long as the customer data used in the promotions is general and we are not using the data we know about a customer’s purchasing habits, likes etc. in order to promote BM. With rider app users it’s ok as long as they have not opted out of the offers. Again please refer to the [+Initial set of rules for targeting Bolt platform users+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-ZJb66nxTKVWqY6lUdsvJsYfd8WOR_lsZsz8Z4yws2c/edit]

# *Promoting Bolt Market to retail users, meaning to any BF users that have made at least one order from a grocery/retail provider in the Bolt Food app. Branding would be from Bolt Market.*

Same answer as for Q1 and Q2.

All of it is OK to do, as long as the customer data used in the promotions is general and we are not using the data we know about a customer’s purchasing habits, likes etc. in order to promote BM. Again please refer to the [+Initial set of rules for targeting Bolt platform users+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-ZJb66nxTKVWqY6lUdsvJsYfd8WOR_lsZsz8Z4yws2c/edit]

# *Promoting a specific Retail provider but only if the provider pays us to be included in the emails/push notifications. Target: Retail users who have made at least one order from any grocery/retail provider. Branding would be from Bolt Food.*

In cases where our partners pay for us directly or indirectly in order to be promoted in the Bolt Food app or in push notifications the [+EU regulation of DSA art 26+ |https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R2065&qid=1666857835014]applies, meaning we must disclose to the user that the ad was sponsored by a restaurant or retail provider. In this case following information about the sponsored content should be disclosed to the user at the latest in the Bolt Food app (if it is not possible or reasonable to disclose this info in the push notification) :

# indication that the information is an ad (for example tag or button named "ad" or "sponsored");
# name of whose behalf the ads are presented;
# name of the person who paid for the ads (if it’s different from the above);
# meaningful information directly and easily accessible from the advertisement about the main parameters used to determine the recipient to whom the advertisement is presented and, where applicable, about how to change those parameters 

See for example how Wolt is doing it:

!IMG_1289.png|width=16.666666666666664%,alt="IMG_1289.png"!

!IMG_1290.png|width=16.666666666666664%,alt="IMG_1290.png"!



!IMG_1291.png|width=16.666666666666664%,alt="IMG_1291.png"!



*Just to note that our product team is working with building the system in order to add the aforementioned information in the Bolt Food app in the near future.* 

Since emails are out of scope for DSA art 26 then it’s just necessary to have an option to “unsubscribe” from receiving the promotional messages. But they don’t need to explicitly say that it is sponsored content. Although it is not legal requirement, then we still recommend to be transparent with the users and if it is reasonable from marketing side then add a very short disclaimer noting that the content in the email is sponsored.

# *Promoting several Retail providers in one email, highlighting the most popular/highest rated providers. Newsletter format. Target: 1) all active Bolt Food users in the city (at least 1 order in the last 90 days), 2) active retail users in the Food app (at least 1 retail order in the last 90 days), 3) Rider app users. Branding would be from Bolt Food.*

It is OK, but similarly to Q4, if the content featured in the emails is sponsored by a retailer, then we should be transparent about it, though it’s not a legal obligation. 

# *Promoting the launch of a big retail brand (e.g. Carrefour, Tesco). Target: All active Bolt Food users in the city (at least 1 order in the last 90 days). Branding would be from Bolt Food.*

Yes that’s OK

For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

# negative balance after a payout is absolutely normal in a market where drivers have a lot of cash rides, for example lets say the month starts on a monday, commission is 10%
1st to 7th driver earns
200 in cash > commission 20
300 in in-app payments > commission 30
Payout> 300-30-20= 250
on next Monday the payout of 250 is sent out to the driver
on the 8th (Monday of the new week) driver does cash rides for 300 > commission 30
in app for 100 > commission 10
End balance for that day = 100 - 10 -30 -250 = -190

If driver doesn't do any rides during the new week, after the payout is deducted from the current balance, balance would stay 0, if the driver wouldn't do _any_ cash rides during first few days of the week, balance would stay positive (in app rides sum is always bigger than commission sum) but as soon as driver has cash rides as well, there is a likelihood that the balance will dip into negative, even without considering payouts in the equation

Hi [~accountid:6242fffc1da0e10071388193]and [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3] , I wanted to draw your attention to this case, as there is a risk of having a Child Maintenance authority visiting our premises.

*Summary of the request:*

* This is a request from a child maintenance authority, and we pushed back on the request based on the quoted legal basis, which we can’t rely on to disclose the data, as the section of the law they are basing their request on is directed at an employer, which we are not.
* There is a threat that an officer intends to visit our premises and they have stated that they can apply for a judicial warrant if not to visit the premises also. There is also threat of fine.

*Next steps:*

* I have analyzed the law that they are referring to ([https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2551/regulation/4/2022-05-26|https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2008/2551/regulation/4/2022-05-26|smart-link] ), specifically, section 4(2) (b) and (c).
* While section 4(2)(b) refers to the employer’s obligations, section 4(2)(c) refers to a person for whom the non-resident parent is providing or has provided services under a contract for services.
* Based on the above, and having in mind the sensitivity of the case + threat of a fine, I will instruct the CS to disclose the data, having in mind that the authority generally has these powers and they might have mistakenly referenced a wrong section of the law they are acting under: Instead of 4(2)(b) they should have referred to 4(2)(c). In addition, have a legitimate interest to defend ourselves against claims, therefore, we can rely on LI as an additional legal basis.
